After a while, midnight boomed from the tall tower at Westminster, and the night seemed to shudder with every resonant stroke. Then the railway lights went dark, leaving a single lamp shining like a great ruby on an enormous mast, and the city’s roar grew fainter.

At two o’clock he rose and wandered toward Blackfriars. Everything looked so unreal, so like a strange dream! The houses across the river seemed constructed from darkness. It was as though silver and shadow had created the world afresh. The vast dome of St. Paul’s appeared through the dim air like a bubble.

Nearing Cleopatra’s Needle, he noticed a man leaning over the parapet. As he drew closer, the man looked up, and the gaslight fell directly on his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the palm reader! There was no mistaking that fat, slack face, those gold-rimmed glasses, the sickly, feeble smile, the sensual mouth.

Lord Arthur stopped. A brilliant idea struck him, and he slipped quietly up behind the man. In an instant he had grabbed Mr. Podgers by the legs and hurled him into the Thames. There was a crude curse, a heavy splash, and then silence. Lord Arthur peered anxiously over the edge, but all he could see of the palm reader was a tall hat spinning in a swirl of moonlit water. After a while that too sank, leaving no visible trace of Mr. Podgers. Once he thought he glimpsed the bulky, misshapen figure swimming toward the steps beside the bridge, and a dreadful sense of failure swept over him. But it proved to be only a reflection, which disappeared when the moon emerged from behind a cloud. At last, it seemed, he had fulfilled destiny’s decree. He released a deep sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name rose to his lips.

“Have you dropped something, sir?” a voice suddenly asked behind him.

He turned to find a policeman carrying a bull’s-eye lantern.

“Nothing important, sergeant,” he replied with a smile. He hailed a passing hansom cab, climbed in, and told the driver to take him to Belgrave Square.

During the following days he swung between hope and fear. At moments he almost expected Mr. Podgers to walk into the room; at others he felt that Fate could never treat him so unjustly. Twice he visited the palm reader’s address in West Moon Street, but could not bring himself to ring. He yearned for certainty and dreaded it.

At last it came. He was drinking tea in the club’s smoking room, listening with some weariness as Surbiton described the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter entered with the evening newspapers.

“One more word, Rose. Dearest Rose, just one more!” Harry cried, throwing himself in front of her. “If I had been less—less fortunate, as the world would call it—if I had been destined for some quiet, obscure life—if I had been poor, ill, helpless—would you have turned away from me then? Or is it my likely rise to wealth and distinction that has created this objection?”

“Do not force me to answer,” Rose replied. “That situation does not exist and never will. It is unfair, almost unkind, to insist on it.”

“If your answer is what I hardly dare to hope,” Harry replied, “it will cast a little happiness along my lonely road and light the way ahead. It is no small thing to do so much, with a few short words, for someone who loves you more than anything. Oh, Rose, in the name of my passionate, lasting love, in the name of everything I have suffered for you and everything you condemn me to endure, answer this one question!”

“Then, if your circumstances had been different,” Rose answered, “if you had been above me only a little, instead of so far; if I could have helped and comforted you in some modest life of peace and seclusion, instead of being a stain and a burden among ambitious, distinguished people, I would have been spared this ordeal. I have every reason to be happy, very happy, now; but then, Harry, I admit I would have been happier.”

As Rose made this admission, memories of old hopes she had cherished long ago as a girl crowded her mind. They brought tears, as old hopes do when they return withered, and the tears gave her relief.

“I cannot help this weakness, and it only strengthens my resolve,” Rose said, holding out her hand. “I really must leave you now.”

“I ask for one promise,” Harry said. “Let me speak to you about this once more, and only once—within a year, say, though it may be much sooner—for the last time.”

“Not to urge me to change a decision I know is right,” Rose replied with a sorrowful smile. “That would be useless.”

“No,” Harry said. “To hear you repeat it, if you choose—repeat it finally! I will place whatever position or fortune I have at your feet; and if you still hold to your present decision, I will do and say nothing to change it.”

“Then let it be so,” Rose answered. “It is only one more pain, and by then I may be better able to bear it.”

She held out her hand again.

It was well after noon when he woke. His valet had tiptoed into the room several times to see whether he was stirring, wondering why his young master was sleeping so late. At last the bell rang. Victor entered quietly, carrying a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small tray of antique Sèvres china, and drew back the olive satin curtains, with their shimmering blue lining, from the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked sleepily.

“A quarter past one, Monsieur.”

So late! He sat up, sipped his tea, and sorted through the letters. One, from Lord Henry, had been delivered by hand that morning. He paused, then set it aside. He opened the rest without interest. They held the usual assortment of cards, dinner invitations, tickets for private exhibitions, charity concert programs, and similar things that descend on fashionable young men every morning during the season. There was a rather substantial bill for an engraved silver Louis XV dressing-table set. He had not yet found the courage to forward it to his guardians, who were extremely old-fashioned and failed to understand that we live in an age when unnecessary things are our only necessities. There were also several very politely phrased letters from moneylenders in Jermyn Street, offering to advance any amount at a moment’s notice and at the most reasonable interest rates.

After about ten minutes he got up, slipped on an elaborate cashmere dressing gown embroidered with silk, and entered the bathroom with its onyx floor. The cool water refreshed him after his long sleep. He seemed to have forgotten everything he had experienced. Once or twice he felt a vague sense of having played a part in some strange tragedy, but it had the unreality of a dream.

When he was dressed, he went into the library and sat down to a light French breakfast, laid out for him on a small round table beside the open window. The day was exquisite. The warm air seemed heavy with spices. A bee flew in and hummed around the bowl decorated with blue dragons that stood before him, filled with sulfur-yellow roses. He felt entirely happy.

Suddenly he noticed the screen he had placed in front of the portrait, and he gave a start.

“Too cold for Monsieur?” his valet asked, setting an omelet on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I’m not cold,” he murmured.
